blocks.text: The accusative answers *kogo? co?*, “whom? what?” Its main job is the direct object of a verb: *zgubiłem plecak*, *kupię bilety*, *poproszę kawę*. It also follows prepositions that express direction and purpose, and it’s used for some expressions of time.

For many nouns the accusative looks like another case, the nominative or the genitive. The real work is knowing which one, and that depends on gender and on whether the noun refers to a person or animal.
Endings: singular

head: accusative
examples
rows: *sobotę, stronę, ulicę, kolację, butelkę, godzinę, nadzieję*

blocks.text: Masculine nouns in *-a* (*kolega*, *mężczyzna*) take the feminine *-ę*, but an adjective with them follows the masculine animate pattern: *mojego kolegę*.

blocks.caption: Adjectives and possessives
head: accusative
examples
rows: *złą stronę, całą sobotę, ślepą uliczkę, w Grodzką*

blocks.text: Endings: plural
The plural has only two patterns. Groups of men (virile) take the genitive form; everything else takes the nominative form:

head: accusative
examples
rows: *bilety, jajka, cytryny, kanapki, buty, życzenia, święta*

blocks.text: Adjectives follow the same split: *moich kolegów* (virile) but *nowe buty* (non-virile).
Exceptions to watch

A number of everyday masculine nouns for things take the animate *-a* in the accusative: *napisać maila*, *wysłać SMS-a*, *zjeść banana*, *grać w tenisa*. This is especially common with games, dances, brands and some recent loanwords. Both *napisać mail* and *napisać maila* are correct.
Pronouns
The short forms *cię* and *go* are the everyday ones; the long forms carry emphasis or start a sentence. After a preposition, third-person pronouns gain an *n-*: *dla niego*, *na nią*.
Direction vs. location
Several prepositions take the accusative when they express movement towards something, and another case when they express being there:
The question tells you which case: *dokąd?*, “where to?”, takes the accusative; *gdzie?*, “where?”, takes the locative or instrumental.
Other prepositions with the accusative

head: preposition
meaning
examples
rows: *chodzi o wykład* · *prosić o pomoc* · *pytać o drogę*
*dziesięć sztuk za dwanaście złotych* · *dziękujemy za zaproszenie*

blocks.text: *O* and *po* change meaning with the case: *o* + accusative is “for, about (asking)”, *o* + locative is “about (talking)”: *chodzi o wykład* but *rozmawialiśmy o wykładzie*. *Po* + accusative is “to fetch”, *po* + locative “after” or “around”: *po powrocie*, *po mieście*.
Time without a preposition
How long something lasts can be a bare accusative: *całą sobotę*, “all Saturday”; *dwa tygodnie*, “(for) two weeks”; *cały dzień*, “all day.”
When the accusative disappears
Negate the verb and the accusative object becomes genitive: *mam czas* → *nie mam czasu*. See the genitive page for details.
